newsitem.title: UK: Clarke says Britain mustn't dither on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Clarke says Britain mustn't dither on EMU.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Sunday it would be the "worst policy" for Britain to dither and then join a European monetary union late.

But speaking on BBC radio, he also said he did not think it would be in Britain's interest to join a new version of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a currency grid that would pave the way for countries to join EMU in later stages.

"That (dithering on EMU) would be the worst policy of all with the British doing their traditional business of not being able to make their minds up and then joining late. That I think would be pathetic," he said.

Clarke, speaking after European finance ministers met this weekend in Dublin, said he did not feel it would be in Britain's interests to join a proposed "ERM II" for countries waiting to join European monetary union after the initial launch.
"I just don't think that's suitable for the United Kingdom. I don't contemplate going into a second ERM if we stay outside," he said.
Britain withdrew sterling from the original ERM in September 1992 after intense speculation in foreign exchange markets pushed it lower.

Finance ministers meeting in Dublin agreed on the architecture of a new currency grid to be set up after European monetary union (EMU) to limit fluctuations between the newly-launched Euro single currency and currencies waiting to join when their economies are ready.
The informal talks in Dublin, which included central bank governors, laid the foundations for three critical areas of monetary union, taking a giant leap towards the realisation of a single currency.

But Britain's Conservative government has retained the right to opt out of any single currency and the party wrangles internally between pro-Europeans such as Clarke and right-wing "Eurosceptics" who want the government to reject EMU.
Last week, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind bolstered Eurosceptic confidence with a keynote speech warning that EMU could tear Europe apart.
Clarke said on Sunday that Britain should make its choice on whether to join in EMU "at the most sensible moment," which he suggested was around a year before EMU went ahead.

"At the most sensible moment, which is the last possible moment to exercise our option, the British should take advantage of the fact that we have a choice as to whether we should join or not," he said.
He added whether Britain should join or not "can only be decided about 12 months before the players are going ahead."
